sections.body: FIRST LAW (inertia): an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity, unless a net (unbalanced) force acts on it. That's why you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.
SECOND LAW: net force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). The same push accelerates a light object more than a heavy one. Force is measured in newtons (N).

THIRD LAW: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. Rockets push gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.
The two forces in the third law act on DIFFERENT objects, which is why they don't cancel out.
Seatbelts work against the first law: they apply the force that stops your body when the car stops suddenly.
Push a light box and a heavy box with the same effort. Which speeds up more? Which law explains it?

quiz.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg object. What is its acceleration?
hints: Example: 30 N on a 6 kg mass → a = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 m/s². Now do 20 N on 4 kg.

quiz.q: You lurch forward when a bus suddenly brakes. Which law explains this?
hints: Your body was moving with the bus.
What does an object do if nothing stops it?
A ball on a smooth floor keeps rolling until friction stops it. Which law is that?
quiz.explain: Your body keeps moving forward (inertia) until a force, like a seatbelt, stops it. That's the first law.

quiz.q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water and moves forward. This is an example of…
hints: The swimmer pushes on the water. What does the water do?
When you jump off a small boat, the boat moves backward. Which law pairs forces like that?
quiz.explain: The swimmer pushes the water back, and the water pushes the swimmer forward: equal and opposite forces (third law).
